questions.question: In the given context, what does the predicate **M(x)** represent?

options.C: x is a student in this class

questions.explanation:
The notation M(x) is defined as “x has visited Mexico.” (Source Page: [22])  

---

questions.question: Which of the following correctly translates the English sentence “Every student in this class has visited either Canada or Mexico”?
questions.explanation:
The correct translation uses implication and a disjunction: ∀x (S(x) → (C(x) ∨ M(x))). (Source Page: [22])  

---

questions.question: Which statement illustrates the “common mistake” of using “∧” as the main connective with a universal quantifier?
questions.explanation:
Example 5 shows that “∀x At(x , HCOE) ∧ Smart(x)” wrongly asserts everyone is at HCOE **and** everyone is smart. (Source Page: [22])  

---

questions.question: How is the sentence “Some student in this class has visited Mexico” expressed in predicate logic?
questions.explanation:
The existential quantifier with conjunction correctly captures “some student … has visited Mexico.” (Source Page: [22])  

---

questions.question: From the premise ∀x (D(x) → C(x)) and the fact D(Marla), which rule allows us to infer C(Marla)?
questions.explanation:
Step 2 instantiates the universal, and Step 4 applies Modus Ponens to obtain C(Marla). (Source Page: [25])  

---

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct translation of “Everyone likes McDonalds”?
questions.explanation:
The proper form is ∀x (likes(x, McDonalds)), as shown in Example 3. (Source Page: [22])  

---

questions.question: In the derivation shown, what is the result of applying Universal Instantiation to the premise ∀x (D(x) → C(x))?
questions.explanation:
Universal Instantiation yields the instance D(Marla) → C(Marla). (Source Page: [25])  

---

questions.question: In Example 20, which conclusion correctly follows from the premises “A student in this class has not read the book” and “Everyone in this class passed the first exam”?
questions.explanation:
The combined premises lead to “Someone who passed the first exam has not read the book,” i.e., ∃x (PassedFirstExam(x) ∧ ¬B(x)). (Source Page: [25])  

---

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the error in the statement “∀x At(x , HCOE) ∧ Smart(x)”?

options.A: It uses implication instead of conjunction.
options.B: It incorrectly places the quantifier only on the first conjunct.
options.C: It asserts a universal conjunction rather than a conditional relationship.
options.D: It omits the variable x in the second predicate.

questions.explanation: The error is that the statement asserts “everyone is at HCOE **and** everyone is smart,” rather than the intended conditional “if someone is at HCOE then they are smart.” (Source Page: [22])
